T1.text:
Okay, so from our table’s perspective, the biggest issue with the survey was how abstract some of the questions felt – particularly around “improvement.” Knowing what we’re improving *from* – a baseline performance level - is absolutely crucial. We also found it unsettling that the survey always framed things as adding data, rather than considering simplifying the model for fairness or privacy reasons.

We all agreed that protecting sensitive data – especially age, gender and race/ethnicity – is non-negotiable. And we strongly feel that any outreach *must* be personalised and supportive, not just automated flagging. Finally, we didn’t see enough emphasis on advisor capacity; a good system needs adequate resources to deliver genuine support.

Building on S1's excellent summary, I would add that the survey lacked sufficient nuance regarding data security assurances. Students need confidence their information is protected, and this wasn’t adequately addressed. We also felt there was a missed opportunity to explore proactively *removing* potentially biased or problematic data sources – focusing solely on additions feels short-sighted. 

Furthermore, while the intervention options were helpful, they didn't fully capture the potential benefits of peer support networks. Finally, we collectively believe the survey underestimated the impact of this system on student wellbeing—the risk of increased anxiety and stigma needs careful consideration throughout the design process.

T2.text:
Okay, here's our table’s report for the plenary, starting with my contribution:

“Our table found the questions around explainability – Q4 – particularly challenging. The levels felt abstract and hard to relate to real student experience. We all agreed that ‘moderate’ or ‘low’ explainability are unacceptable; clarity is paramount, even if it means identifying fewer students. 

The biggest difference in responses was regarding selectivity for generic emails (Q7.1). I initially prioritised reach, but others rightly pointed out the risk of overwhelming students. Ultimately, we agree prioritizing clear communication and a supportive tone – alongside high explainability – are key to building trust and ensuring this system actually *helps* students.”

Building on S4’s excellent summary, I'd add that we identified a crucial gap in the survey: it didn’t adequately address ongoing monitoring of the model for bias *after* deployment. Ensuring fairness isn’t a one-time fix; it requires continuous assessment and adjustment.

We also felt Q6 – interventions – lacked nuance. More detailed options, encompassing timing and advisor training on sensitive delivery, would have been valuable. Finally, we agree prioritizing high explainability isn't simply about technical accuracy. It’s fundamentally about building trust, minimizing anxiety, and recognizing the diverse needs of our student population – a human-centered approach is essential.”

T3.text:
Okay, here’s our table's report – my draft for the plenary:

Hi everyone. Our table found Q5 and Q7 were the most challenging. In Q5 on fairness, defining “student groups” was crucial but vague – we need clarity there. We all agreed on prioritising both identifying students needing help *and* avoiding false positives, especially for vulnerable groups. 

Q7 about selectivity sparked debate. I initially favoured fewer contacts due to potential stress, but we recognised advisors see many struggling in silence. The biggest takeaway is the absolute need for student agency – an opt-out system and clear communication before any personalised outreach are vital. We felt the survey lacked options around those safeguards. Ultimately, wellbeing and respectful support must come first.

Building on S7’s excellent summary, I'd add that we felt the survey underestimated the importance of resource limitations. We discussed interventions a lot – personalised emails and meetings are great, but only if advisors have the capacity to respond effectively! That wasn’t reflected in the questions.

Also, while Q6 touched on interventions, it lacked nuance around tailoring support. Different students need different things; study skills workshops aren't helpful for everyone. And finally, regarding fairness, we strongly felt the survey focused too much on *outcomes* – equal identification rates - and not enough on the potential for bias in the data itself. We need proactive steps to mitigate that risk during model development, which wasn’t explicitly addressed.
